1.explanation: Harriet 先说成 Carridge，随即更正并拼写 K-E-R-R-I-D-G-E。不要填 Carridge 或 Harriet。

3.explanation: 她原想订 11 May，但 Marcus 说那一期已满，改订 18 May。不要填 11 May 或 25 May（候补日期）。

4.explanation: 宣传是 2 o’clock，但 Marcus 说明实际从 2.15 开始，以便先做安全须知。不要填 2.00 或 2 o’clock。

5.explanation: 工作日才有 hand-building；她要订的周六课是 wheel throwing。不要填 hand-building 或 pottery。

6.explanation: 标准费用是 £37.50。优惠价 £29 仅给学生和六十岁以上人士，她不符合。不要填 29 或 45（材料押金）。

7.explanation: 中心提供围裙和粘土，不要自带粘土。Marcus 建议带一件 old shirt 以免溅到衣服。不要填 apron 或 clay。超过两个词（如 an old shirt）按词数限制判错。

8.explanation: 她说朋友提起过网站，但她实际是在图书馆海报上看到课程。不要填 website 或 friend。

9.explanation: Marcus 先提到中心收费停车场，随后说明周六下午 1 点后 Maple Street 路边免费，并建议她把车停在那里。超市停车场只给顾客用。故选 A。

10.explanation: 姐姐喜欢陶艺只是闲聊；她明确说想先试一次，再决定要不要参加周二晚的常规课。不是为了做生日礼物或开店。故选 C。

11.explanation: 咖啡馆紧挨主楼东侧，对应图上 A。不要与主楼内的咨询台混淆。

12.explanation: 展览厅在主楼正北、通往木栈道的路上，对应 B。

13.explanation: 观鸟屋在泻湖北岸东端，对应 C。不要把北面沙嘴上的瞭望塔 F 当成观鸟屋。

14.explanation: 野餐草坪在主楼西侧，对应 D。西北角的 Play area 已标出，不是本题。

15.explanation: 船库在东岸，靠近泻湖，对应 E。

16.explanation: 瞭望塔在北面沙嘴上，对应 F。与观鸟屋 C 是两处不同地点。

17.explanation: Guided beach walks 只在周末进行。不是会员专属，也不需要提前预约。

18.explanation: Kayak hire 必须提前预订，因为名额有限。不要选周末才有或会员专属。

19.explanation: 望远镜可凭入场票免费借用。先提到押金是干扰，随后说明凭票即可。

20.explanation: Evening talks 只在七月和八月举办。今年没有取消。

21.explanation: Tomás 提到电脑出过问题，Jade 说只做了两周，但导师指出真正的问题是数据只覆盖午餐、没有晚餐。故选 B。

22.explanation: Tomás 先建议称未上桌的食物，讨论后他们决定称盘子里剩下的食物。故选 A。

23.explanation: 导师反对在排队时采访，也反对把问卷做得太长，要求采访不超过十分钟。故选 C。

24.explanation: 问卷由 Aisha 来写；Jade 主动承担海报设计。联系厨房经理尚未有人接下。故选 B。

25.explanation: 系研讨会名额已满；他们改在校园可持续发展集市上展示。不是投稿学生期刊。故选 C。

26.explanation: 秤已经可以借用，学生参与也不太令他们担心；最大的顾虑是厨房员工是否合作。故选 A。

27.explanation: 文献综述由 Tomás 来写。他先推给 Aisha，后接受了。

28.explanation: 伦理表格由 Aisha 完成，因为她做过类似表格。

29.explanation: 预研究（pilot study）由 Jade 来做。

30.explanation: Aisha 先说她去订会议室，后因要交伦理表改由 Tomás 预订。不要选 C。

31.explanation: 泥炭地变干是因为十九世纪修建了 drains。后面出现的 ditches 是早期田间沟，不是本题所要的词。

32.explanation: 干泥炭会向空气中释放 carbon。同句提到 heat 和 dust，但笔记对应 releases ... into the air 的是 carbon。

33.explanation: 讲者先说 buildings，随即更正为 roads，并补充 bridges。笔记是 local ______，标准答案为 roads。填 roads and bridges 超过两个词，判错。

34.explanation: 有人以为是 2011 年，但讲者说明水泵实际在 2009 年关闭。不要填 2011 或 2012。

35.explanation: 水位现由 sluice gates 控制。pumps 已经关掉，不是现行控制方式。

36.explanation: 工程暂停是因为 lapwings 正在筑巢。geese 很多但不是停工原因。

37.explanation: 农民得到的补偿是湿草甸上的 hay，可以出售；不是现金补贴。

38.explanation: 出乎意料回归的是 eels。otters 是预期中的，不是 unexpected。

39.explanation: 当前研究在测量 methane 排放。carbon 已在前面作为干泥炭的问题出现，不是正在测量的对象。

40.explanation: 访客中心的资金被取消，改为修建一条 boardwalk。不要填 visitor centre。

Narrator: This is the Academic Listening practice test, Set A.

Narrator: Section 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman and a receptionist at a community arts centre.

Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

Marcus: Good morning, Elmwood Community Arts Centre, Marcus speaking. How can I help you?

Harriet: Oh, hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your weekend pottery workshops, please.

Marcus: Of course. Let me take a few details. Can I start with your name?

Harriet: Yes. It's Harriet Carridge. Sorry — not Carridge. It's Kerridge. That's K-E-R-R-I-D-G-E.

Marcus: Kerridge. Thank you. And a contact number, in case we have to change anything?

Harriet: My mobile is 0 7 7 5 4, 6 2 9 8 1 3. No, wait, I've got that back to front. It's 0 7 7 5 4, 6 2 9 1 8 3.

Marcus: 0 7 7 5 4, 6 2 9 1 8 3. I've got that. Now, the workshops. We still have space on the 18th of May, and there's a later date, the 25th, if you'd rather.

Harriet: I was hoping for the 11th of May, actually. That's the first Saturday I have free.

Marcus: I'm afraid the 11th is already full. We keep a short waiting list, but I wouldn't count on a place. The 18th of May is the next one, and that's the one I'd recommend.

Harriet: That's fine. Please put me down for the 18th of May.

Marcus: Done. The advertised start time is 2 o'clock, but I should tell you that we actually begin at 2.15. We use the first quarter of an hour for a safety briefing, and we found people were turning up just as that finished. So please arrive by 2.15, not 2 o'clock.

Harriet: 2.15. That's helpful, thank you. And is it a hand-building class? That's what a friend of mine did on a weekday.

Marcus: The weekday evenings are hand-building, yes. The Saturday workshop is wheel throwing. You get a proper go at the potter's wheel, with a tutor beside you. We don't mix the two on the same day.

Harriet: Wheel throwing. That's exactly what I wanted.

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

Narrator: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

Harriet: Can I just check the price? I thought I saw 29 pounds somewhere.

Marcus: The concession fee is 29 pounds, but that's only for full-time students and for people over 60. The standard fee is 37 pounds 50. There's also a 45-pound materials deposit on the wall chart, but you can ignore that — we stopped taking a deposit last year.

Harriet: I'm not a student, and I'm certainly not 60, so it'll be 37 pounds 50 then.

Marcus: That's right. You can pay when you arrive. Now, what to bring. We supply aprons, and we supply all the clay, so please don't bring your own — it can clog the wheels. The one thing I do suggest is an old shirt, because even with an apron you can get splashes on your sleeves.

Harriet: An old shirt. Easy enough. Oh, and you asked on the website how people find you. A friend did mention your site, but I didn't actually book from there. I saw a poster in the library and rang you from that.

Marcus: A library poster. That's useful to know — we've just put those up. A couple of last things. Parking: we do have a small paid car park behind the building, but on Saturdays after 1 p.m. you can park for nothing on Maple Street, right beside the entrance. I'd use that. The supermarket across the road looks convenient, but they only allow their own customers to park there, and they do check.

Harriet: Maple Street after 1. Perfect. I'll do that.

Marcus: And just out of interest, is this a one-off, or are you thinking of joining a regular group?

Harriet: My sister is the one who loves pottery — it's her birthday soon, and she keeps making bowls. I did think about making her something, but I'm not at that stage. I'm not planning to sell anything either. I really just want to try the wheel and see whether I'd enjoy the Tuesday evening class later in the year.

Marcus: That's a very good way to start. I'll email your confirmation this afternoon. We look forward to seeing you on the 18th.

Harriet: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

Marcus: Goodbye.

Narrator: That is the end of Section 1. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers.

Narrator: Section 2. You will hear a welcome talk for visitors at a newly opened coastal visitor centre.

Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.

Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.

Lena Pritchard: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Saltmarsh Coastal Visitor Centre. My name is Lena Pritchard, and I'm the visitor services officer here. The centre only opened in March, so you're among our first guests, and I'm going to start by walking you through the plan you have in front of you, so you can find your way around.

Lena Pritchard: You come in at the south, at the bottom of the plan, past the entrance, and the first building you reach, in the middle of the site, is the main building. That's where the information desk is, and it's already labelled. If you go just to the right of that building, to the east, you'll see a smaller, low structure attached to it. That's the café. It's marked A on your plan. We serve drinks and light meals there until 4 o'clock, and you can sit inside or on the terrace.

Lena Pritchard: Directly north of the main building, on the path that leads up towards the water, is a long, low hall. That's the exhibition hall, letter B. It tells the story of the saltmarsh and the people who have worked here, and I do recommend you start there before you walk out to the lagoon.

Lena Pritchard: Now, the lagoon itself fills most of the north of the site, at the top of your plan. If you follow the boardwalk — that's already labelled — along the water, you'll come to a small wooden shelter on the north-east shore. That's the bird hide, letter C. It's a quiet place, and we ask you not to use flash photography in there. People sometimes assume the hide is the tall structure on the little spit of land further north, but it isn't. I'll come to that in a moment.

Lena Pritchard: Coming back inland, to the west of the main building, there's an open grassy area. That's the picnic lawn, letter D. It's the best place for a packed lunch, and it's more sheltered than it looks. Please don't picnic on the play area just north-west of it — that's already labelled, and it's for children. There's also a first-aid post near the entrance, which is marked on your plan, and the car park is in the south-west corner.

Lena Pritchard: Two more outdoor buildings. On the eastern shore of the lagoon, along the path that leaves the exhibition hall, you'll find the boat shed, letter E. That's where we keep the kayaks and the shallow-water boats. And finally, on that narrow spit of land that sticks out into the lagoon at the very north of the plan, there's a slim wooden tower. That's the lookout tower, letter F. You get a wide view of the incoming tide from the top, and, as I said, it isn't the bird hide — the hide is the low shelter to the east.

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

Narrator: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.

Lena Pritchard: Let me tell you briefly about some of the activities you can join while you're here. First, the guided beach walks. These are popular, and we used to offer them every weekday, but we simply don't have the rangers for that now. They run at weekends only. You don't need to be a member, and you can just turn up at the entrance at 10 o'clock — no booking is required.

Lena Pritchard: Kayak hire is a different matter. We have only a small number of kayaks, and for safety we need a staff member on the water with you. So kayak hire must be booked in advance, either at the desk or on the website. It isn't limited to members, and we do hire them on weekdays as well as at weekends, provided a guide is free.

Lena Pritchard: If you want a closer look at the wading birds, we lend out telescopes. I should have said we were going to charge a deposit for those, but we dropped that idea. Telescope loans are free with the admission ticket. Just leave your ticket at the desk and collect it when you bring the telescope back. Members don't get any extra privilege there — the same rule applies to everyone.

Lena Pritchard: And finally, our evening talks. A few people have asked whether these have been cancelled this season. They have not. What we have done is concentrate them in the summer, when the days are longer and the café can stay open afterwards. So the evening talks run in July and August only. They're included in a separate small fee, and they're open to visitors as well as members.

Lena Pritchard: That's all I wanted to cover this morning. Please come and find me if you have any questions, and enjoy your visit to Saltmarsh.

Narrator: That is the end of Section 2. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers.
transcripts.3:
Narrator: Section 3. You will hear a tutor, Dr Brennan, and three students, Jade, Tomás and Aisha, discussing a research project on food waste in a university cafeteria.

Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.

Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.

Dr Brennan: Thank you for coming in. You've chosen to follow up last year's study of food waste in the cafeteria, which is a good idea, but I want to be sure you don't repeat its mistakes. Tomás, you looked at the old data. What was the main problem?

Tomás: Well, their laptop did crash at one point, and they had to re-enter some figures, but I don't think they actually lost the file. And Jade noticed they only sampled two weeks, which is short, but they did both weeks properly.

Jade: Yes, two weeks in November. The real gap, though, is what you pointed out in your notes, Dr Brennan.

Dr Brennan: Go on.

Jade: They only collected data at lunchtime. The cafeteria is open for dinner as well, and the amount of waste might be quite different then. So the set is incomplete.

Dr Brennan: Exactly. The main weakness is that the data were collected at lunchtime only. If you run this again, you must cover the evening service too. Now, how do you want to measure the waste?

Tomás: I thought we could weigh the food that never leaves the kitchen — the trays that are prepared and then thrown away unsold. That seemed tidy.

Aisha: It's tidy, but it doesn't tell us what students actually leave. I'd rather weigh the leftovers on the plates when they come back.

Jade: I agree with Aisha. The kitchen already has a rough idea about unserved food. The interesting question is what people put on a plate and then don't eat.

Tomás: Fair enough. Let's do the leftovers on the plates. We can still glance at the unserved trays, but we won't use them as the official measure.

Dr Brennan: Good. And interviews? Aisha, you wanted to talk to students in the queue.

Aisha: I thought we might catch them while they're waiting, and I drafted about twenty-five questions so we wouldn't miss anything.

Dr Brennan: Two problems there. People in a queue are in a hurry, and a long interview will irritate them and give you poor answers. Keep the interviews to no more than ten minutes, and do them at a table, after they've sat down, not in the line. You can cut that list of questions in half.

Aisha: Ten minutes. I'll trim it.

Dr Brennan: Who is doing what, practically? The questionnaire, the poster for the fair, contacting the kitchen?

Aisha: I'll write the questionnaire, since I'm cutting it down anyway.

Jade: Then I'll design the project poster. I did the poster for the geography display last term, so I already know the template.

Tomás: We still need someone to speak to the kitchen manager. I can try, but I haven't met her.

Dr Brennan: Leave that for now — I may be able to introduce you. Let's talk about where you'll present the findings. The departmental seminar would have been ideal, but those slots are already full this term.

Tomás: Could we send it to the student journal? They sometimes take short research notes.

Aisha: They take months to reply. The campus sustainability fair is in May, and they'll give us a stand if we apply this week.

Jade: That's better. We'll present at the sustainability fair.

Dr Brennan: Good choice. And what's the thing that still worries you most?

Tomás: Borrowing the weighing scales was my worry, but the lab technicians have already said yes.

Jade: I'm not too concerned about student numbers either. People like being asked about food.

Aisha: The kitchen staff are the unknown. If they think we're criticising their work, they may not let us stand by the racks and weigh anything. That's what I keep thinking about.

Dr Brennan: That's a fair concern, and it's the one I'd watch too. I'll help with that introduction. All right, let's assign the remaining tasks.

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

Narrator: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.

Dr Brennan: You still need a short literature review, an ethics form, a pilot study, and a room to meet in each week. Let's not leave those hanging.

Tomás: Aisha is better at the reading than I am. Could she do the literature review?

Aisha: I've already got the questionnaire and the ethics form in my head. I really can't take the review as well.

Dr Brennan: Tomás, the review isn't a huge piece of writing. I'd like you to do it. You've already looked at last year's study, so you're halfway there.

Tomás: All right. I'll write the literature review.

Aisha: And I will complete the ethics form. I submitted one for my interview project last year, so I know the wording they want.

Dr Brennan: Good. The pilot study — a short trial in the cafeteria, maybe two days, before the main count. Jade?

Jade: Yes, I'll run the pilot study. I can do that in the first week of April, before the main data collection.

Aisha: And I'll book the meeting room. I pass the office every morning.

Tomás: Are you sure? Once you start on the ethics form, you usually disappear for a week.

Aisha: That's true. I might be chasing signatures. Tomás, could you book the meeting room instead? You're in that building on Tuesdays anyway.

Tomás: Yes, I'll book the meeting room. Leave it with me.

Dr Brennan: Excellent. Email me the plan by Friday, and we'll meet again after the pilot.

Jade: Thank you, Dr Brennan.

Narrator: That is the end of Section 3. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers.

Narrator: Section 4. You will hear a lecture about a peatland restoration project on the Fenmere Levels.

Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

Professor Whitby: Good afternoon. In this lecture I want to examine a restoration project on the Fenmere Levels, a lowland peat landscape about thirty kilometres from here, and to consider what it can tell us about the wider problem of drying peat soils.

Professor Whitby: Let me begin with some background. For centuries the Levels were wet. Farmers cut small ditches by hand to move water short distances, and those early ditches are still visible in places. The real change came in the nineteenth century, when engineers constructed a network of drains — deep, straight channels that carried water off the land and into the river. Once those drains were in place, the peat began to dry.

Professor Whitby: A dry peat soil has several costs. It blows away as dust in a warm spring, and it no longer holds the cool moisture that neighbouring fields depend on. Most seriously, dried peat releases carbon into the air, as the plant material that was locked up under water begins to break down. That carbon loss is now a measurable part of the region's emissions.

Professor Whitby: There is a physical cost as well. As the peat dries, the ground shrinks and sinks. I nearly said this had damaged local buildings, and in a few villages garden walls have cracked, but the more serious and widespread damage has been to local roads. Several stretches have had to be rebuilt, and a couple of small bridges have been affected too. When you complete the notes, the word you want for that damaged infrastructure is roads.

Professor Whitby: Now to the project itself. People often date it to 2011, because that was when the first public report appeared, or even to 2012, when the visitor signs went up. In fact the pumps were switched off in 2009. That is the year the restoration really began, quietly, by allowing water to stay on the land instead of being lifted away.

Professor Whitby: The pumps have not been used since. Water levels are now controlled by sluice gates, which can be raised or lowered to hold a steady depth across each block of land. That is a gentler and cheaper method than pumping, and it has proved surprisingly precise.

Professor Whitby: The work has not been without interruption. The Levels are full of geese in winter, and visitors often assume that the geese caused the main delay, because they graze the new shoots. In fact the project had to pause because of nesting lapwings. These birds nest on the bare, wet ground in spring, and a construction team cannot move in beside them. The lapwings, not the geese, were the reason work stopped for two seasons.

Professor Whitby: Farmers, naturally, wanted to know how they would be paid. An early proposal offered a cash subsidy for every hectare left wet, but that scheme was never adopted. Instead, farmers are compensated with a crop of hay. The wet meadows produce a late, high-quality hay which they can sell on, and that has turned out to be more popular than a cheque, because it keeps them in the farming business.

Professor Whitby: The wildlife response has been encouraging. Otters were expected to return, and they have done so, along the main channels. The unexpected arrival has been eels. Nobody had recorded eels on the Levels for nearly forty years, and they appeared in the second summer after the pumps stopped. That is the species to note as unexpected.

Professor Whitby: Research is still going on. We already know, as I said, that dry peat releases carbon, so that is not the current question. What the team is measuring now is methane emissions. A wet peatland can give off methane, and we need to be sure that we are not simply trading one greenhouse gas for another. The early figures are reassuring, but the measurements will continue for several years.

Professor Whitby: Finally, access for the public. The original plan included a small visitor centre at the eastern car park. That funding was withdrawn last year, and the centre will not be built. What is going ahead is a boardwalk, raised above the wettest ground, so that people can reach the lagoon edge without disturbing the birds or sinking into the peat. If you remember only one planned visitor facility, it should be the boardwalk.

Professor Whitby: I'll stop there, and in the seminar we'll look at how these lessons are being applied to two other lowland sites.

Narrator: That is the end of Section 4. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers.

Narrator: That is the end of the listening test. In the full test you will now have two minutes to check all your answers.
